BLK.name: BlackRock
BLK.numbers_line: EPS $15.93 vs $14.32 est (beat, +38% y/y); revenue $7.75B vs $7.42B est (+19%); net inflows $205B, organic base-fee growth 11%, operating margin 47.8% (+320bp), AUM $15.5T.
BLK.guidance: At least $550M of buybacks in Q4; tax ~25%; G&A up mid single digits; ACV growth low-to-mid teens long term. Q4 is the seasonal peak (30–40% of iShares annual flows) and private-markets fundraising should be stronger than Q3; evergreen private funds expected to 'turn a corner' in Q4 and H1 as higher base rates bring allocators back to private credit.
call_said: Fink: 'For the first time in my career… I'm seeing genuine shortages of capital.' Federal deficits and the AI build-out are competing for the same money, which he says means structurally higher rates for longer, especially at the long end. His answer is to turn compute into an asset class the way mortgages became MBS: a 1 GW data centre is ~$50B, 40% of it GPUs, and start-ups without ratings will need asset-backed chip financing. BlackRock is 'presently in the market with a very large transaction'.

Deals named: Meta's $14B Texas data centre financed with GIP and HPS, the ~$40B Aligned Data Centers close through the AI Infrastructure Partnership, Humana and AT&T financings, an $80B Dutch pension mandate. Kapito: the ten-year above 5%, real rates near 3%, 'bonds are back' is early innings; fixed income took $78B in the quarter.

Where the ETF money went: index bond ETFs $61B, precision $41B, active a record $22B, digital assets $8B; semiconductor and South Korea ETFs were among the highest-inflow products. Institutional index equities saw $27B of outflows. Tax-aware long-short strategies ($19B AUM, $4B inflows) are bumping into custodian capacity limits.
BLK.quote: "For the first time in my career, and that's 50 years of a career, I'm seeing genuine shortages of capital." — Larry Fink
BLK.read_through: The crowd is in semis and Korea through ETFs, so the memory trade (MU, SNDK, the hynix and Samsung read) is now a flow trade as well as a fundamental one. The biggest allocator says rates stay high: that is the discount-rate headwind on every long-duration name in the universe.

FAST.name: Fastenal
FAST.numbers_line: EPS $0.35 vs $0.34 est (beat); revenue $2.46B vs $2.44B est; sales +15.5%, operating margin 21.5% (+90bp), the largest year-over-year operating-income gain in a quarter in the company's history; ROIC 32.5%.
FAST.guidance: No formal guidance. 27,000–29,000 FMI device signings and $310–330M of capex for the year held. Gross margin carries a structural 50–60bp mix headwind from large customers; price/cost neutrality plausibly by Q1 2027. Internal standard: 10% top-line growth in any environment with mid-20s incremental margins; pricing's contribution (2.4% this quarter) keeps fading as 2025 increases lap.
call_said: Data centres are now 4–5 points of growth, served through contractors and the suppliers building them, with on-site 'pods' set up to keep pace with demand that is 'sometimes pretty overwhelming on the speed'. Heavy manufacturing (~45% of sales) grew ~20%; US PMI averaged nearly 55.

September daily sales of 14.4% came in below normal seasonality for the first time in months: described as moderation from very strong levels while lapping pricing, with pockets of weakness in ag and food, resellers and government. Diesel inflation is real and the captive fleet mitigates it; IEEPA tariff refunds were immaterial.

Labour is the structural story: sales-force headcount down over 400 since June while FTEs grew under 1%; an AI quoting tool took sourcing-and-quoting from 5–6 days to 15 minutes; branch managers now ask for a tool instead of two or three heads. A small AI-orchestration acquisition was made and not disclosed because of size.
FAST.quote: "Now those same managers, they're calling in and saying, 'Hey, we don't need the 2 or 3 heads. We need this tool.'" — Jeff Watts
FAST.read_through: The cleanest industrial read of the week: manufacturing demand improving, data-centre construction visible in a fastener distributor's growth, and labour productivity from AI already in the margin. Supports the data-centre build names (VRT, PWR, FIX on 22 Oct) and the industrials reporting this week (GE, MMM, HON).

MS.name: Morgan Stanley
MS.numbers_line: EPS $3.03 vs $2.93 est (beat); revenue $20.3B vs $19.9B est; ROTCE 22.6%, a fifth straight quarter above 20%; wealth net new assets a record $232B with $80B of fee-based flows; equities $5.8B (+41%).
MS.guidance: Wealth NII up modestly in Q4 and expanding in 2027 on loan growth; Q4 tax rate slightly above Q3, full-year unchanged; wealth pre-tax margin (30.4%) expands with scale, no quarterly target; 300bp of excess CET1 kept as 'substantial flexibility' pending the final capital rules.
call_said: Ted Pick's framing: the quarter had two phases, a brisk July–August on hyperscaler AI spending, then post-Labor Day headwinds from the Middle East and higher global rates; volumes 'drying up in Asia' in September. 'Glass mostly full' (US nominal GDP 5–6%, full employment) versus 'half empty' (conflicts, meaningfully higher rates and energy, a fourth year of a bull market) will decide behaviour into H1 2027.

AI capex: hyperscaler spend running ~ $1 trillion a year, worth 50–70bp of US real GDP; MS was 'overweight' AI and is now 'double overweight', with a warning that some bridge loans will become equity and get provisioned: 'we are going to make mistakes'. IPO-related flows (SpaceX among them) were just over half of the record net new assets.

Sponsors: some are 'stuck on marks and MOICs that are just not going to come to pass' in the new cost-of-capital regime; strategics, not sponsors, lead the cycle. Deposits were deliberately grown $30B to $465B to fund the bank; the funding benefit shows up in 2027.
MS.quote: "I would say that we were overweight. And… I would say we are now double overweight." — Ted Pick, on AI coverage and risk capital
MS.read_through: A trillion a year of hyperscaler capex is the demand line under NVDA, AVGO, MU and TSM; the IPO funnel (SpaceX) is a universe-level liquidity event. The caution is the same as Dimon's and Solomon's: financing mistakes will be made, and they land first on the neo-clouds and bridge-financed builders.

BNY.name: BNY
BNY.numbers_line: EPS $2.37 adjusted vs $2.27 est (beat, +24% y/y; $2.34 reported); revenue $5.68B vs $5.55B est (+12%); pre-tax margin 39%, ROTCE 29%, ~390bp of positive operating leverage.
BNY.guidance: Raised again: 2026 revenue growth around the middle of 12–13% ex notables, NII +15%, positive operating leverage ~500bp (was 400bp three months ago and ~100bp in January), expense growth around the middle of 7–8%. Q4 fees 'flattish, not down'; Q4 expense step-up is seasonal, not a jump-off point for 2027.
call_said: AI at scale: $4B a year of technology spend inside a $13B expense base, 400-plus AI solutions in production on the Eliza platform, framed as 'capacity' not efficiency. Vince on token economics (model routing, open-weight models, 'you don't need a sledgehammer to crack a nut') and on alignment and observability needing to catch the frontier; BNY opened an AI lab at Carnegie Mellon.

Rates: BNY 'narrows the cone' and is largely immunised to ±100bp; ~$5B of securities roll off each quarter and reinvest at a 150→200bp yield pickup; deposits dipped seasonally in Q3 and are already picking up in Q4. Collateral balances a record $8.3T (+14%); Treasury central clearing is volume, not a headwind.

Tokenisation is in production: a digital transfer agency, the BLIQUID tokenised Dreyfus money fund, BlackRock and Baillie Gifford share classes on it, Pay-to-Wallet cross-border payments. Issuer Services fees +43% partly on pass-through revenue as financial agent for Trump Accounts; Wealth Solutions (ex-Pershing) net new assets $48B, 7% annualised.
BNY.quote: "At BNY, AI is for everyone, everywhere and everything." — Robin Vince
BNY.read_through: The market's plumbing is growing double digits on volumes and debt issuance, which is the activity read for SCHW, CME (21 Oct) and the exchanges. Tokenised funds are live at the largest custodian, which is the institutional side of the story HOOD (27 Oct) and the crypto names trade on.

MRSH.name: Marsh (Marsh McLennan)
MRSH.numbers_line: Adjusted EPS $2.03 vs $1.97 est (beat, +10%); revenue $6.86B vs $6.64B est (+8%, +5% underlying); adjusted operating income +6%, margin flat at 22.7%.
MRSH.guidance: Full-year underlying growth similar to 2025, another year of margin expansion, solid adjusted EPS growth. Thrive savings target raised to $600M from $400M (costs ~$750M, actions mostly done by end-2028). ~$5.5B of capital deployed in 2026 across dividends, M&A and buybacks ($2B repurchased year to date). Q4 management consulting roughly flat on success-fee timing; fiduciary income ~$94M.
call_said: Insurance pricing is falling: the Marsh global index −5% in Q3 after −6%, global property −10%, cyber −4%, US casualty +1% but US excess casualty +13% on loss-cost inflation; reinsurance soft with abundant capacity through the 1 January renewals. Reinsurance revenue −6% in a small quarter, −1% year to date.

AI as revenue: Oliver Wyman's Quotient AI-transformation practice is the fastest grower (management consulting +14%, some success fees pulled from Q4); brokers are pushing back on blanket AI exclusions in policies; Marsh launched the Stratus Exchange, up to $10B of property capacity for operating data centres, after the $2.7B Nimbus construction facility. Doyle flagged AI-driven cyber exposure as a systemic worry.

The Middle East is a named drag (workforce & rewards −1%, 2,500 colleagues in the region); levered PE-owned brokers face soft pricing plus higher rates, which Marsh sees as talent and 'string of pearls' M&A opportunity rather than a reason to answer Aon's large deal. A $144M litigation settlement closed the GREG/SILL case.
MRSH.quote: "This change is structural, not cyclical, and it is happening at pace and all at once." — John Doyle
MRSH.read_through: Softer commercial insurance pricing is a cost tailwind for every insured and a top-line headwind for carriers: read for TRV (reported 16 Oct), PGR and CB (tonight). The data-centre insurance facilities are the unglamorous enabler of the build-out the chip names depend on.
